# Diagnosing Intermittent Power Failure in a Mercedes C180 Compressor

A car refusing to start despite a seemingly healthy battery is a classic diagnostic headache, particularly when the failure appears intermittent. In the specific case of the Mercedes C180 Compressor described, the vehicle failed to crank initially, requiring an external jump-start via ADAC. The fact that the battery was nearly new and showed no warning flags on the dashboard suggests we are dealing with a transient voltage collapse or a parasitic drain issue rather than a simple dead cell failure.

The core technical question here is how a vehicle can start immediately after being jumped but fail again later. This behavior often points to a voltage-dependent protection mechanism within the ECU (Engine Control Unit) or a failing battery management system. Modern ECUs, including those in Mercedes-Benz models, monitor battery voltage continuously. If the voltage drops below a specific thresholdâoften around 9V or 10V during crankingâthe ECU may enter a "limp mode" or shut down to protect its internal hardware. When an external battery is connected, it raises the system voltage well above this threshold. However, if the primary battery has lost its ability to hold a charge (internal resistance has increased significantly) or if there is a parasitic load keeping the resting voltage low, the car will appear fine at rest but fail under load. This explains why the car started after the jump but potentially failed again later; the underlying chemical degradation of the battery cells meant it could not sustain the voltage required for the ECU to stay online once the external aid was removed or if the state-of-charge dropped too quickly during driving.

A critical clue in this scenario is the observation that shifting into reverse (R) activates the multimedia system/radio when it is off. This is a strong indicator of a parasitic drain issue or a glitch in the CAN bus communication logic. In many modern vehicles, the transmission control unit signals the infotainment system to wake up based on gear selection. If the battery voltage sags even slightly during this transition, or if the grounding path is compromised, the ECU might misinterpret the signal state, causing peripherals to power up unexpectedly. While not always dangerous, this behavior suggests that the electrical architecture is operating near its failure point. The "almost new" battery could be suffering from sulfationâa condition where lead sulfate crystals form on the plates due to deep discharge cycles or leaving the car with a low charge, effectively shortening the battery's lifespan regardless of its age.

To prevent recurrence, the first step is verifying the health of the alternator and the charging system. If the alternator is not maintaining the battery at 13.5Vâ14.7V while the engine runs, even a brand-new battery will die within hours. Next, perform a parasitic draw test. Disconnect the negative terminal and place an ammeter in series to measure current flow with the car fully off. A healthy resting draw should typically be under 50mA. Anything higher indicates a component staying powered or a short circuit.

Furthermore, inspect the ground straps and battery terminals for corrosion or loose connections. High resistance at the connection points can cause significant voltage drops during high-current events like cranking, triggering the ECU's low-voltage protection even if the battery itself holds charge. In cases where the battery was replaced by the manufacturer (as in the update), monitor the new unit closely. If the issue persists with a known good battery and alternator, investigate the CAN bus gateways or the specific control modules that handle gear-to-infotainment signaling, as a software glitch could be mimicking hardware failure.

If you are maintaining your own fleet or building custom vehicles with complex electrical systems, logging voltage data during these events is invaluable. Using an oscilloscope to capture the voltage dip at the moment of cranking can reveal exactly when the ECU cuts power. This data-driven approach prevents guessing and ensures that the root causeâwhether chemical degradation in the battery or a logical fault in the control unitâis addressed directly.
